result.summary: Pausanias describes the grove of Pelops at Olympia, its rites, and the story of Pelops' shoulder-blade, which was needed to take Troy and was later recovered by a fisherman. He then describes the great altar of Zeus at Olympia, made of ash and the debris of thigh bones, and its yearly renewal.

scenes.title: The grove and cult of Pelops
scenes.summary: The walled grove of Pelops in the Altis is described, along with the black ram sacrificed there and the taboo on those who eat of it.

scenes.title: The shoulder-blade of Pelops
scenes.summary: Seers say Troy could not fall without the bow of Hercules and a bone of Pelops. The bone was lost in a wreck, fished up by Damarmenus, and given to the Eleans on Delphi's advice.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks cannot take Ilium, and Elis suffers a pestilence, unless the bone is found and kept.

scenes.title: Traces of Pelops in Asia
scenes.summary: Pausanias cites the Tantalus marsh and grave, the throne of Pelops on Sipylus and the myrtle Aphrodite at Temnus as signs of Pelops' Asian origin.

scenes.title: The altar of Olympian Zeus
scenes.summary: The ash altar of Zeus is described: its origin, measurements, who may climb it, and its yearly renewal with Alpheus water. Similar altars at Pergamum, Samos and Didymi are mentioned.

alias_notes.explanation: Some say the altar was built by an Idæan Hercules, a figure of Cretan tradition distinct from the son of Amphitryon.
Hercules the son of Amphitryon, born at Thebes.

notable_quotes.reason: Pelops is ranked among Olympia's heroes as Zeus is among the gods.

analysis.text: Hero cult and ritual: Pelops receives chthonic-style sacrifice, with taboos that mark him off from the cult of Zeus.
Pausanias gathers relics and local traditions as evidence of Pelops' Asian origins, reflecting how Greek cities used heroes' bones and tombs to claim legitimacy.

legacy.text: Pelops is the eponym of the Peloponnese, and the Olympic Games were later linked to his cult.

fun_facts.text: The ash altar of Zeus at Olympia has not survived; Pausanias is the main source for its dimensions and ritual.

language_notes.text: Altis was the sacred precinct of Olympia, enclosing the temples, altars and statues; the name is the local word for the grove.
The 'trench' refers to a pit for offerings to a hero, as distinct from the raised altars used for the gods.
'Has no portion' means the seer receives no share of the victim, a usual perquisite elsewhere.
Telephus was a mythical king of Mysia, worshipped at Pergamum; the passage compares his cult's ritual restriction to that of Pelops.
Ilium is Troy. The prophecy says Troy needed the bow of Hercules, held by Philoctetes, and a bone of Pelops.
The Pythian Priestess was the oracle of Apollo at Delphi.
"Brought colonies" means led settlers from Asia Minor into Greece; Pausanias reads the Asian place-names as evidence of this migration.
Pelops sought Hippodamia's hand by winning a chariot race against her father Oenomaus; he first sought Aphrodite's favour.
Idæan Hercules is the Cretan Heracles of Mount Ida, a figure distinct from Hercules the Theban, son of Alcmena.
"Débris" here means the ash and remains from burnt thigh bones, which were packed together to form the altar.
"Extemporary altars" are makeshift altars of ash or rough material, improvised rather than built with finished stone.
"Pro-altar" is the broad lower base (prothysis) where the victims were slaughtered, in front of the upper altar.
"Seers" are the prophets (manteis) of Olympia, here charged with the annual renewal of the altar.

context_notes.text: Hercules was a descendant of Pelops through Amphitryon's ancestry, which explains why he would honour him with a precinct.
Philoctetes inherited Hercules' bow and had been left behind on Lemnos; the Greeks fetched him to Troy. Pisa is the territory around Olympia.
Eretria was a city on the island of Euboea (spelled Eubœa here), so the lost bone drifted near its own coast.
Sipylus is a mountain in Lydia, in Asia Minor, Pelops' reputed homeland; Temnus lay near the river Hermus.
Women were barred from the Olympic Games at certain times, so access to Olympia was restricted by sex and season.
Didymi was the site of Apollo's famous sanctuary near Miletus, a Greek city on the coast of Asia Minor.

literary_notes.text: The prophecy that Troy needs a relic of Pelops sets up the later story of the bone's wreck and recovery.
The fisherman's catch and his awe at the bone's great size give a vivid, concrete picture suggesting a heroic past.
Chance appears providential: the Eleans happen to be at Delphi just when the bone's owner is to be identified.
Pausanias adds a personal judgement, 'in my opinion', typical of his travelling, sceptical guide voice, explaining why the relic is gone.
The river Alpheus is called "friendly" to Zeus, giving the stream a divine favour and an attitude toward the god.
The brief aside distances Pausanias from the Milesian claim, showing his habit of reporting local traditions without endorsing them.
Pausanias dryly undercuts the Milesians' claim by noting that the blood altar has never grown tall, implying doubt.
